_note: Habit anchors. The cue never changes; the reason rotates. Rationales are written to be true rather than persuasive -- where the evidence is thin the card says so, because a claim Seth later finds was oversold poisons every other claim in the library.

morning_light.action: Sky, not sun. Five to ten minutes. No sunglasses.
morning_light.optional: Optional: a few poses out there, shirt off.

why.hook: Here's the switch almost nobody flips.
why.why: Light hitting your eyes in the first hour after waking is the single strongest signal your circadian clock takes. Not caffeine, not food, not movement. Light.

why.hook: Here's the number that should annoy you.
why.why: A bright indoor room is 100 to 300 lux. Outside on an overcast morning is 1,000 to 10,000. Direct sun is over 50,000. Your kitchen is not a substitute; it is two orders of magnitude short.

why.hook: Here's the cell you didn't know you had.
why.why: Your retina has receptors that do nothing for vision. They exist only to tell your brain what time it is. They are most sensitive to the blue-heavy light of morning sky.

why.hook: Here's what you're actually setting.
why.why: Morning light advances your clock, which pulls tonight's melatonin release earlier. You are not waking yourself up. You are scheduling tonight's sleepiness.

why.hook: Here's the one that costs you nothing.
why.why: Five to ten minutes on a clear morning. Fifteen to twenty if it's grey. That's the whole intervention.

why.hook: Here's the mistake that wastes the whole thing.
why.why: Window glass cuts the intensity hard, and you are usually further from the light than you think. Through a window is a fraction of the dose. Go outside.

why.hook: Here's the accessory that cancels it.
why.why: Sunglasses defeat the point. Contacts and clear glasses are fine. This is the one time of day you want your eyes uncovered.

why.hook: Here's what you never look at.
why.why: Never look directly at the sun. You don't need to. Sky, not sun — the ambient field is what carries the dose.

why.hook: Here's why the grey days matter most.
why.why: Overcast still delivers many times what your ceiling light does. The mornings you'd skip are the mornings the gap between inside and outside is widest.

why.hook: Here's the trade that beats duration.
why.why: Ten minutes every morning beats forty minutes twice a week. This system responds to consistency, not to volume.

why.hook: Here's the second lever, free.
why.why: Cortisol has a natural spike shortly after waking — it is supposed to happen. Morning light sharpens it, which is why the day starts cleaner and the evening crash is less abrupt.

why.hook: Here's the one that compounds.
why.why: Every morning you anchor the clock, the next night's sleep onset gets a little more predictable. This is the input with the longest tail in the whole system.

why.hook: Here's what the winter version looks like.
why.why: Shorter days means less signal, later. Going out at the same clock time matters more in January than in July, not less.

why.hook: Here's the sequencing most people get backwards.
why.why: Light first, then coffee. Caffeine masks the adenosine you should be clearing with light. One is a signal, the other is a mute button.

why.hook: Here's the cheap upgrade.
why.why: Face east if you can see the horizon. Low-angle morning light is spectrally different from midday and it is exactly what the system evolved on.

why.hook: Here's the honest limit.
why.why: This will not fix a bad night. It sets the phase of tomorrow's night. Judge it over two weeks, not over one morning.

why.hook: Here's the version for a bad start.
why.why: Overslept, rushed, no time? Thirty seconds on the step still beats zero. The dose is graded, not all-or-nothing.

why.hook: Here's what it does to sleep onset.
why.why: A clock that is properly anchored in the morning stops drifting later. Drift is why bedtime creeps and why you lie there awake.

why.hook: Here's the mood note, stated carefully.
why.why: Bright light in the morning has real evidence behind it for mood, strongest in seasonal low mood. Not a treatment. A tailwind.

why.hook: Here's the pairing that stacks.
why.why: Movement in the light beats light alone — temperature, heart rate and the clock all get the same message at once. A slow walk is enough.

why.hook: Here's the shirt-off version.
why.why: Skin exposure adds vitamin D synthesis to the light dose. Low-angle morning sun is the safest window for it. Optional, not the point.

why.hook: Here's the yoga version.
why.why: A few poses outside turns a two-minute errand into a ritual. Rituals survive bad weeks; errands don't.

why.hook: Here's what to do when there's no sun at all.
why.why: Still go out. Cloud cover changes the intensity, not the fact that outside beats inside by a factor you cannot make up indoors.

why.hook: Here's the identity, not the tactic.
why.why: People who sleep well are outside within an hour of waking. Not because they're disciplined. Because it became the first thing they do.

blue_blockers.action: Blue blockers until you're asleep. Overheads off if you can.

why.hook: Here's the wavelength that does it.
why.why: The receptors that tell your brain what time it is peak around 480 nanometres — the blue-cyan band. Evening light in that band reads as daytime.

why.hook: Here's what's actually well established.
why.why: Evening light suppresses melatonin. That part is solid and repeatable. The glasses are one way to cut it, and they are the cheapest.

why.hook: Here's the honest caveat, up front.
why.why: Evidence that blockers improve sleep is thinner than the internet suggests — small trials, mixed results. The mechanism is sound, the effect size is uncertain. It costs almost nothing, so it stays.

why.hook: Here's the mistake in the product category.
why.why: Faintly yellow 'computer glasses' block very little. If the lens isn't visibly amber or orange, it is mostly reassurance.

why.hook: Here's the thing that beats the glasses.
why.why: Turning the overhead lights off does more than any lens. Glasses are the backup when you can't control the room.

why.hook: Here's the timing.
why.why: Two to three hours before bed is the window that matters. Yours is 7:30 for a 22:30 target. Earlier is fine; later is mostly wasted.

why.hook: Here's the source you're ignoring.
why.why: Your ceiling light is probably brighter than your phone. People blame screens and sit under a 1,000-lumen fixture.

why.hook: Here's the geometry nobody mentions.
why.why: Light from above hits the lower retina, where those clock receptors are densest. Overhead lighting is worse than a lamp at eye level for the same brightness.

why.hook: Here's the second job the glasses do.
why.why: Putting them on is a cue. It tells your own nervous system the day is closing. Half the value is the ritual, and that half is real.

why.hook: Here's what 'night mode' is worth.
why.why: Screen colour shifting reduces the blue fraction but not the total brightness, and brightness matters too. It is a partial measure, not a solution.

why.hook: Here's the compounding cost.
why.why: Melatonin release delayed by an hour tonight is not an hour of lost sleep tonight — it is a clock that starts drifting later all week.

why.hook: Here's the dose relationship.
why.why: Intensity and duration both matter, not just wavelength. Two hours of dim beats twenty minutes of bright. Blocking the whole evening beats blocking the last ten minutes.

why.hook: Here's the one that surprises people.
why.why: Melatonin isn't a sedative. It's a timing signal. Suppressing it doesn't make you less tired — it makes your body think it's earlier than it is.

why.hook: Here's the test you can run yourself.
why.why: Two weeks on, two weeks off, same bedtime, and watch your sleep latency. You have 1,000-plus nights of baseline. You can actually answer this for yourself.

why.hook: Here's the failure mode.
why.why: Glasses on, then three hours under bright lights on a screen until midnight. The lens is not a licence. It is a reduction on top of an already-dim evening.

why.hook: Here's the cheapest version of all.
why.why: Lamps instead of ceiling lights, and put them low. Free, permanent, and it works whether or not you remember the glasses.

why.hook: Here's what the ancestral argument is worth.
why.why: Fire is warm-spectrum and dim. Every artificial light before about 1880 was. That's context, not proof — but the direction of the evidence agrees with it.

why.hook: Here's the compliance trick.
why.why: Keep them where the evening starts, not by the bed. A habit that needs you to walk somewhere is a habit that fails.

why.hook: Here's the individual-variation caveat.
why.why: Sensitivity to evening light varies a lot between people — several-fold in the same conditions. You might be at either end. That is what your own two-week test would tell you.

why.hook: Here's what it buys the morning.
why.why: Protecting tonight's melatonin onset makes tomorrow's wake time easier. The evening habit and the morning habit are the same lever from opposite ends.

why.hook: Here's the bit about alertness.
why.why: Evening light doesn't only shift the clock; it acutely increases alertness. Some of what keeps you up isn't the melatonin, it's the light saying 'stay awake'.

why.hook: Here's the version for a social evening.
why.why: Out with people, no glasses? Fine. Get them on when you're home. A partial evening is not a failed one.

why.hook: Here's the honest ranking.
why.why: Dim the room. Then get off overhead lighting. Then the glasses. Doing only the third is doing the weakest one.

why.hook: Here's the identity, not the tactic.
why.why: People who sleep well treat the last three hours as part of the night, not the end of the day. The glasses are just the visible edge of that.
